## Signed, not yet in force

| State | Law | Starts | What changes |
|---|---|---|---|
| CO | [SB 26-189](/colorado/sb-26-189/) | **Jan 1, 2027** | Pre-use notice, 30-day adverse-outcome disclosure, human review |
| CO | HB 26-1263 (Chatbot Safety) | Rules pending | Age estimation, non-human disclosure, suicide protocols |
| NY | RAISE Act | Jan 1, 2027 (registration from Nov 2026) | Frontier developer registration, 72-hour incident reports |
| NY | S9051B | Jan 1, 2027 | Age assurance for AI companions used by minors |
| CA | SB 942 phase 2 | Jan 1, 2027 | Large online platforms + GenAI hosting platforms |
| CA | CCPA ADMT rules | Jan 1, 2027 | Risk assessments, pre-use notices, opt-out for significant decisions |
| CA | SB 947 | Jul 1, 2027 | No sole reliance on automated systems for discipline or termination ($500/violation) |
| CA | SB 1119 ("Adam's Law") | Jul 1, 2027 | Child risk assessments for companion chatbots |
| CA | SB 942 phase 3 | Jan 1, 2028 | Capture-device duties |

---

## Barred by court order — do not build compliance around these

| Law | Status | Why |
|---|---|---|
| [CA AB 2839](/california/ab-2839/) | **Permanently enjoined** | First Amendment. Judgment Aug 29, 2025. California did not appeal this ruling. |
| [CA AB 2655](/california/ab-2839/) | **Preempted by §230, barred against all platforms** | Judgment Aug 20, 2025; stipulated order Aug 28, 2025. Appeal pending, No. 25-6138, no argument date. |
| CO SB 24-205 | **Repealed before taking effect** | Replaced by SB 26-189 on May 14, 2026. Never operative. |

---

## What this table is not

It is not every AI law in the country. It covers **disclosure and transparency** obligations — the laws that require you to tell someone something — plus the prohibitions that travel with them. Bias-audit laws, procurement rules, and state-agency governance are tracked separately.

It also does not cover the roughly 26 states with narrow **election deepfake** statutes. Those bind campaigns rather than businesses and are handled in a separate section.

---

## Frequently asked questions

**How many states require AI disclosure?**
Six states have enforceable disclosure or transparency duties as of November 2026. Colorado joins them on January 1, 2027. More than 26 additional states have narrow election-deepfake disclosure rules.

**Is the Colorado AI Act in effect?**
No. The 2024 law never became operative. The replacement, SB 26-189, starts January 1, 2027. → [Full explanation](/colorado/)

**Can I rely on California's AB 2839 or AB 2655?**
No. Both are barred by court order. Use Elections Code §20010 and AB 2355 instead. → [What still applies](/california/ab-2839/)

**Do any of these require a bias audit?**
Not among the disclosure laws. New York City's Local Law 144 requires one for automated employment decision tools; that is a city ordinance, not a state AI disclosure law.

**What is the single strictest disclosure duty in the country right now?**
For scope, Colorado from January 1, 2027 — every deployer, every covered domain, with a 30-day post-decision explanation.

---

**Start here:** [Illinois HB 3773](/illinois/hb-3773/) · [Colorado](/colorado/) · [California SB 942](/california/sb-942/) · [Texas TRAIGA](/texas/traiga/) · [Utah](/utah/) · [Maine](/maine/chatbot-disclosure/) · [New York](/new-york/synthetic-performer/)

*Last verified November 8, 2026. General information, not legal advice. This table is updated as laws change; if you spot an error, the official source on each state page controls.*


<!-- https://aidisclosurelaw.com/maine/chatbot-disclosure/ -->
# Maine's Chatbot Disclosure Law: No Threshold, No Intent, No Excuses

> **Short answer.** Since **September 24, 2025**, **10 M.R.S. §1500-DD** bars using an AI chatbot — or any other computer technology — to engage in trade or commerce with a consumer in a way that may mislead or deceive a reasonable consumer into believing they are dealing with a **human being**, unless the consumer is notified **clearly and conspicuously** that they are not. No employee threshold. No revenue test. No intent element. No exception for a bot that discloses only after being asked. A violation is a violation of the **Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act**, enforceable by the Attorney General.

Two citation traps sit on top of that: the section was **reallocated from §1500-Y**, and a separate synthetic-media rule for political advertising lives at **21-A §1014(5-C)** and took effect July 29, 2026.

---

## The citation changed, and half the internet missed it

The chatbot rule was enacted as **LD 1727**, signed June 12, 2025, as **P.L. 2025, ch. 294**. It was originally codified at **§1500-Y**.

The Revisor of Statutes then reallocated it. The operative citation is now **10 M.R.S. §1500-DD**, and the published text carries the line "*(REALLOCATED FROM TITLE 10, SECTION 1500-Y)*" at the top.

What that means in practice:

- A policy document or vendor questionnaire citing **§1500-Y** is citing a section that no longer exists under that number.
- Guidance written before late 2025 will often cite §1500-Y **and** describe a weaker duty than the one in force.
- If you are citing a Maine chapter number for this rule, note that the reallocation also carries a revisor's reference to **RR 2025, c. 1, Pt. A, §16** — the statutory basis for the move.

This is the same failure mode as Utah's §13-2-12: a real law, an obsolete citation, and a corpus of articles that never got updated.

---

## What the statute actually says

Two elements, and both are broader than the equivalent text in other states.

| Element | Language and effect |
|---|---|
| **The technology** | "Artificial intelligence chatbot" means a software application, web interface, or computer program that **simulates human conversation and interaction through textual or aural communications** — and the prohibition reaches "any other computer technology" beyond chatbots |
| **The conduct** | Engaging in trade or commerce with a consumer **in a manner that may mislead or deceive a reasonable consumer** into believing the consumer is engaging with a human being |
| **The escape** | The consumer is notified **in a clear and conspicuous manner** that they are **not** engaging with a human being |
| **The consequence** | A violation **is** a violation of the Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act |

Three details do the work:

**"May mislead" is not "does mislead."** The standard is the capacity to mislead a reasonable consumer, not proof that one was misled. An unnamed assistant with a human name and a friendly avatar is the paradigm case.

**There is no threshold of any kind.** No employee count, no revenue figure, no volume of chats. A two-person business with a website widget is covered on the same terms as a bank.

**No intent requirement.** You do not have to have set out to deceive anyone. The design decision is the violation.

---

## Why geo-targeting is the wrong answer

The natural instinct is to disclose only to visitors in Maine. Two problems:

1. **You usually cannot know.** The state of a visitor is an inference from IP, and a VPN, a corporate proxy, or a mobile carrier makes it wrong. A disclosure that fires on a misread location is worse than none.
2. **The cost of over-disclosure is close to zero.** A line of text telling everyone they are talking to a bot does not measurably hurt conversion on support or transactional flows, and it eliminates the question entirely.

The businesses that get this wrong are not the ones that decided to deceive. They are the ones that shipped a bot with a human persona — a name, a face, a typing indicator, "Hi, I'm Alex!" — and never asked whether Alex was a disclosure problem.

---

## What "clear and conspicuous" looks like in practice

The statute does not define the format. It does define the failure: a consumer who could reasonably believe a human is on the other end. Test your implementation against these:

| Question | Why it decides the case |
|---|---|
| Does the notice appear **before** the first exchange, not after? | A disclosure delivered at message four lets the first three mislead |
| Is it **visible without scrolling or expanding**? | A footnote below the fold is not conspicuous |
| Does it say **"not a human"**, not just "AI-powered"? | "Powered by AI" describes the software; the statute is about who the consumer thinks they are talking to |
| Does it survive the **handoff**? | Human agent → bot is the most common failure. The persona returns; the disclosure does not |
| Does it follow the conversation **out of the widget**? | SMS, email, WhatsApp, and voice all need their own notice |
| Does the voice agent **say it out loud** at the start? | "Textual or aural" is explicit in the definition |
| Does the **human name and avatar** contradict it? | A confident human persona next to a small disclosure line is arguably still misleading |

That last row is the one that ends arguments. Maine's standard is what a reasonable consumer takes away, not what the footer says.

---

## Penalties

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Enforcer | Maine Attorney General |
| Vehicle | Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act, 5 M.R.S. §205-A et seq. |
| Civil penalty | Set by the UTPA's general penalty provision (5 M.R.S. §209), which authorises civil penalties per violation |
| Other relief | Injunctive relief, restitution, and the Attorney General's costs |
| Private right of action | Under the UTPA, not under §1500-DD itself |
| Chatbot-specific fine | **None.** Maine attached the duty to an existing statute rather than creating a new penalty |

Attaching the rule to the UTPA rather than writing a bespoke AI penalty is deliberate, and it has a practical consequence: you are measured against decades of unfair-and-deceptive-practice precedent about what a reasonable consumer understands, not against a new and narrow AI test.

---

## The other Maine rule: synthetic media in political ads

Different chapter, different audience, and it took effect later. **21-A M.R.S. §1014(5-C)**, enacted as **LD 517** (**P.L. 2025, ch. 593**), signed March 23, 2026, and in force **July 29, 2026**.

If a political communication that already requires a campaign-finance disclosure contains synthetic media of a candidate, it must also carry the words:

> THIS COMMUNICATION CONTAINS AUDIO, VIDEO AND/OR IMAGES THAT HAVE BEEN MANIPULATED OR ALTERED

Details that matter:

- **Synthetic media** means an image, audio, or video of a candidate that, in a manner likely to deceive a reasonable person, depicts them saying or doing something they did not, or has been manipulated to give a materially different impression. **Satire, parody, and technical clarity edits are excluded.**
- **The penalty is different from the rest of the section**: up to **500% of the expenditure** on the offending communication, against 100% for other disclosure violations in the same section.
- **Broadcasters and newspapers** are liable only if they publish with **actual knowledge** that the communication contains synthetic media.

This one binds campaigns and committees, not ordinary businesses. It is included because the citation gets confused with §1500-DD constantly, and because the two were enacted a year apart under different public laws.

---

## Implementation checklist

- [ ] Replace every internal reference to **§1500-Y** with **§1500-DD**
- [ ] List every conversational surface: website widget, in-app chat, SMS, WhatsApp, voice IVR, email auto-responders
- [ ] For each, ask the statute's question: could a reasonable consumer think a human is replying?
- [ ] Put the notice **before** the first exchange, visible without scrolling, saying **not a human**
- [ ] Retire or rename human personas that contradict the notice — the avatar is part of the disclosure analysis
- [ ] Write the handoff rule: every bot-to-human and human-to-bot transition re-states the notice
- [ ] Add the notice to outbound channels separately; the widget text does not travel
- [ ] For voice agents, script the spoken disclosure into the opening, before any substantive answer
- [ ] If you run political advertising in Maine, keep the §1014(5-C) wording and the 500% exposure separate from this checklist

---

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the Maine chatbot law in force?**
Yes, since September 24, 2025.

**Is it 10 M.R.S. §1500-Y or §1500-DD?**
§1500-DD. The section was originally codified at §1500-Y and reallocated by the Revisor of Statutes; the current published text notes the move at the top.

**Does the law apply to small businesses?**
Yes. There is no employee or revenue threshold of any kind. Any business using a chatbot in trade or commerce with a Maine consumer is covered.

**Do we have to disclose if the customer never asks?**
Yes. Unlike Utah, Maine's duty is proactive: the notice must be clear and conspicuous before the consumer could be misled, not on request.

**What if our bot only handles order status?**
The test is whether a reasonable consumer could believe they are dealing with a human. A bot that says "I'm the automated order assistant" is fine. One that says "Hi, this is Alex from support" is the fact pattern the statute was written for.

**What is the penalty?**
A violation of §1500-DD is a violation of the Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act, enforced by the Attorney General through the UTPA's civil penalty and injunctive provisions. Maine did not create a chatbot-specific fine.

**Does the political advertising rule apply to businesses?**
No. 21-A §1014(5-C) binds political communications that already require a campaign-finance disclosure, and it carries a 500% penalty on the expenditure. Ordinary commercial chatbots are governed by §1500-DD.

---

**Related:** [Which state AI disclosure laws are in force](/in-effect/) · [Utah chapter 77: reactive vs proactive disclosure](/utah/) · [Illinois HB 3773 notice duty](/illinois/hb-3773/)

*Last verified November 8, 2026. General information, not legal advice. Confirm against the current text of 10 M.R.S. §1500-DD on the Maine Legislature site — the reallocation means older citations point elsewhere.*


<!-- https://aidisclosurelaw.com/new-york/synthetic-performer/ -->
# New York Requires Ads to Disclose AI-Generated Humans

> **Short answer.** **S8420-A / A8887-B**, signed **December 11, 2025** as Chapter 617, in force since **June 9, 2026**, amends **General Business Law §296-b**. If a **visual or audiovisual advertisement** for property or services, in any medium, distributed to a consumer in New York, features a **synthetic performer** — a digitally created human who is not any identifiable real person — the person who produced or created the ad must **conspicuously disclose** that fact, when they have **actual knowledge** of it. Penalties are **$1,000** for a first violation and **$5,000** for each subsequent one, enforced by the Attorney General.

New York is the first state to make the **mere presence** of an AI-generated human in an ad a disclosure trigger, independent of whether the ad is misleading. That is a different regulatory theory from every deepfake law that came before it.

---

## The test is the person, not the picture

Most advertising disclosure rules ask whether the **content** is misleading. This one asks whether a **person in the frame is real**.

| The ad contains | Disclosure required? |
|---|---|
| An AI-generated human holding the product, looking like a model | **Yes** |
| A real actor, background replaced with AI | No — the human is real |
| A product-only shot, AI-generated set | No — no human likeness |
| A real actor, voice translated by AI | No — translation exemption |
| An AI-generated human in a promo for a film or game, used as in the work | No — expressive-work exemption |
| Audio-only ad with an AI-generated voice | No — audio-only ads are excluded |
| A synthetic influencer posting organic-feeling content for a brand | Likely yes, if it is an advertisement reaching New York |

The definition: a **synthetic performer** is a digital asset created, reproduced, or modified by computer using generative AI or a software algorithm, intended to create the impression of an audiovisual and/or visual performance by a human performer **who is not recognizable as any identifiable natural performer**.

The last clause matters. A digital replica of a specific real person is a **right of publicity** problem, not this one. This statute is about the human who is nobody — the AI model, the AI spokesperson, the fabricated presenter.

---

## Why e-commerce is the exposure, not the brand campaign

A national brand shoot with an AI presenter is a one-off decision with a legal review attached. A marketplace with 40,000 listings is a different problem, because the practice arrived quietly:

- AI-generated lifestyle models holding products, replacing photography for cost reasons
- Synthetic presenters in UGC-style video ads, bought in volume from agencies
- AI avatars narrating product tours
- Localised ad creative where the model was regenerated per market

Every one of those is an advertisement featuring a synthetic performer, distributed to a New York audience by default — because no digital campaign can reliably exclude New York, and nobody wants to.

The practical audit is therefore **listing-level and creative-level**, not campaign-level. The question to put to the team is not "did we use AI in this campaign" but "is there a human in this asset, and is that human real".

---

## "Actual knowledge" is in the statute, and it is not a loophole

The duty attaches when the advertiser **has actual knowledge** that the ad contains a synthetic performer.

Read carefully, this is narrower than strict liability and narrower than it first appears — but it is not a defence you want to rely on. Actual knowledge is established by ordinary business records: the vendor invoice that says "AI-generated model", the prompt log, the Creative team's Slack thread, the asset filename. In an organisation that knowingly commissions AI models, knowledge is not seriously contestable.

Where the standard genuinely helps is the **unknowing** case: an agency delivers a shoot and does not disclose that some frames were generated, or a licensed stock library supplies synthetic people without labelling them. The fix is contractual — warranty and indemnity in the production agreement — not a compliance memo.

---

## What "conspicuous" has to mean

The statute requires conspicuous disclosure and does not prescribe wording or placement. Enforcement will be fact-specific, so design to the plainest reading: a viewer who is not looking for a disclaimer should still register it.

| Format | What survives scrutiny | What does not |
|---|---|---|
| Video | On-screen text for the duration of the synthetic performer's appearance, legible at mobile size | A 1-second flash at the end |
| Static image ad | Text on the creative, contrasting, readable at thumbnail size | A caption below the platform's "sponsored" label |
| Social video | Disclosure in the creative itself | Reliance on the platform's own "AI-generated" toggle |
| Carousel / stories | On each frame containing the performer | First frame only |

The platform labelling point is the one teams push back on. Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube all offer AI-content labels, and it is tempting to treat them as compliance. They are not: they are platform policies, applied inconsistently, and visible in different places from the ad. The obligation in §296-b sits with the person who produced the ad.

---

## Who is not liable

The statute deliberately spares the distribution layer. Newspapers, magazines, television networks, streaming services, cable systems, billboard companies, and transit advertisers are **not liable** for publishing or disseminating a non-compliant ad.

That concentrates liability on two parties: the **advertiser**, and the **agency or production company** that created the work. Which is why the second-order effect of this law is contractual — production agreements now need to allocate who warrants that no synthetic performer is present, and who pays if one is.

---

## Penalties

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Enforcer | New York Attorney General |
| First violation | **$1,000** |
| Each subsequent violation | **$5,000** |
| Private right of action | Not created by this section |
| Media outlets / platforms | Exempt from liability for running the ad |
| Other law unaffected | Civil Rights Law §§50, 50-f, 51, and §230 of the Communications Act are expressly preserved |

The penalty amounts are small relative to a national campaign, which is the wrong way to read them. The Attorney General picks test cases, and the second-order cost — re-shooting a catalogue, pulling live listings, restating agency agreements — is where the money is.

---

## The companion law, effective the same day

Governor Hochul signed **S8391 / A8882** at the same time, expanding the **post-mortem right of publicity** under **Civil Rights Law §50-f**. Heirs or executors must consent before a deceased person's name, image, or likeness — including a vocal or visual **digital replica** — is used commercially.

That one took effect **immediately on December 11, 2025**, six months before the advertising disclosure rule. It applies to estates and to anyone producing digital replicas of identifiable people, and it is a separate exposure from §296-b.

Together the two laws cover both halves of the problem: the **identifiable** person (publicity rights, consent, estates) and the **unidentifiable** one (disclosure).

---

## Implementation checklist

- [ ] Classify every live creative: is there a human in frame, and is that human real
- [ ] For each synthetic performer, add a conspicuous on-creative disclosure for the full duration of their appearance
- [ ] Audit product listings and marketplace imagery, not just campaign assets — set a date to finish
- [ ] Do not rely on platform AI labels as the disclosure
- [ ] Put a warranty into production and agency agreements: no synthetic performer without disclosure, with indemnity
- [ ] Require vendors to label synthetic assets at delivery, in the filename and the metadata
- [ ] Add an AI-performer check to the creative approval gate, before trafficking
- [ ] Train media buyers: any placement that can reach New York is in scope, including programmatic
- [ ] Separately review digital replicas of identifiable people under Civil Rights Law §50-f
- [ ] Diary the first enforcement actions; the Attorney General has not yet issued format guidance

---

## Frequently asked questions

**Is the New York synthetic performer law in effect?**
Yes, since June 9, 2026. Signed December 11, 2025.

**Does it apply to companies outside New York?**
Yes. It reaches any advertisement distributed to a New York audience, wherever the advertiser is located. For digital campaigns that effectively means everywhere.

**What exactly is a synthetic performer?**
A digital asset created, reproduced, or modified by computer with generative AI or a software algorithm, intended to look like a human performer who is not any identifiable real person. AI models, AI spokespeople, and fabricated influencers qualify.

**Do we need to disclose if we use AI to retouch a real model?**
No. The trigger is a human who is not real. Enhancing an image of a real person, or replacing a background, does not create a synthetic performer.

**What about audio ads?**
Excluded. The statute covers visual and audiovisual advertising, and audio-only ads are exempt.

**Are the platforms liable if our ad is missing the disclosure?**
No. Media outlets and ad platforms that publish or run the ad are exempt. Liability sits with the advertiser and the producer or creator of the ad.

**What is the penalty?**
$1,000 for the first violation, $5,000 for each subsequent violation, enforced by the New York Attorney General.

---

**Related:** [Which state AI disclosure laws are in force](/in-effect/) · [Illinois HB 3773: the employer notice duty](/illinois/hb-3773/) · [Maine's chatbot disclosure rule](/maine/chatbot-disclosure/)

*Last verified November 8, 2026. General information, not legal advice. Confirm against GBL §296-b as amended and the bill text of S8420-A before relying on an exemption.*


<!-- https://aidisclosurelaw.com/texas/traiga/ -->
# Texas TRAIGA (HB 149): Who Actually Has to Disclose AI

> **Short answer.** TRAIGA took effect **January 1, 2026**. The affirmative **disclosure** duties fall on two groups only: **government entities** using AI to interact with consumers, and **health care providers** using AI in connection with services or treatment. Private companies have **no general AI disclosure obligation** under TRAIGA. What reaches private companies is the prohibition list — behavioral manipulation, unlawful discrimination, CSAM and unlawful deepfakes, and infringement of constitutional rights.

This distinction is the single most common error in TRAIGA coverage. Guides that tell every Texas business to add an "AI disclosure" to its website are describing a law that does not exist.

---

## The disclosure duty, precisely

### Government entities

An agency that makes available an AI system intended to interact with consumers must disclose, **before or at the time of the interaction**, that the consumer is interacting with an AI system.

The disclosure must be **clear and conspicuous** and written in **plain language**. Not buried in a privacy policy, not a footnote in terms of service — at the point of interaction.

### Health care providers

A provider using AI in relation to health care services or treatment must give a clear and conspicuous disclosure to the recipient, or the recipient's personal representative, **not later than the date the service or treatment is first provided**.

**Emergency exception:** where the situation is an emergency, the disclosure is due as soon as reasonably possible.

### Who is not covered by the disclosure duty

Private businesses, unless they are a government entity or a health care provider in the sense the act uses. Note also that "consumer" is defined as a Texas resident acting in an **individual or household context** — it expressly excludes individuals acting in a commercial or employment context. So an employer's AI-driven HR process is not a "consumer" interaction under this definition.

---

## The prohibitions, which do reach private companies

| Prohibition | Who it binds | Intent required? |
|---|---|---|
| Manipulating behavior to incite self-harm, harm to others, or criminal activity | Any person | **Yes** — "intentionally aims to" |
| Social scoring by government | Governmental entity | **Yes** |
| Biometric capture without consent, infringing individual rights | Governmental entity | — |
| Impairing US or Texas constitutional rights | Any person | **Yes** — "sole intent" |
| Unlawful discrimination against a protected class | Any person | **Yes** — disparate impact alone is **not** sufficient |
| CSAM, unlawful deepfakes, explicit conversations impersonating minors | Any person | **Yes** — "with the intent of" |

The intent requirement is the deliberate design choice that separates Texas from Colorado. A model that produces a discriminatory *outcome* is not, by itself, a TRAIGA violation. That is a much narrower law than most summaries suggest — and it is why TRAIGA passed while broader bills did not.

**Exemptions:** certain insurance entities and federally insured financial institutions are exempt, provided they comply with or are regulated by other applicable law.

---

## Penalties

| Violation type | Civil penalty |
|---|---|
| Curable, or breach of a statement submitted to the AG | **$10,000 – $12,000** per violation |
| Uncurable | **$80,000 – $200,000** per violation |
| Continued violation | **$2,000 – $40,000 per day** the violation continues |

Enforcement is exclusively the Attorney General's, who may issue civil investigative demands and seek injunctive relief, attorney's fees, court costs, and investigative expenses. The AG must give **60 days' notice and an opportunity to cure** before enforcement.

**No private right of action.**

---

## Two things people miss

**The AG complaint portal.** TRAIGA required the Attorney General to post an online consumer complaint mechanism by **September 1, 2026**. That is the intake channel that will generate the first enforcement matters. If your organization has a Texas consumer-facing AI product, watch what gets filed there.

**Local ordinances are preempted.** Texas preempts local government AI ordinances. Companies should treat TRAIGA as a single statewide baseline rather than a patchwork of city rules — one of the few places in US AI law where you get uniformity.

**Plus:** TRAIGA creates a regulatory sandbox and the Texas Artificial Intelligence Council, and requires state agencies to report on their AI use through the Sunset Advisory Commission and the Department of Information Resources.

---

## Checklist

**If you are a government entity:**
- [ ] Identify every consumer-facing system that could be characterized as AI
- [ ] Put a clear, plain-language disclosure at the point of interaction — before or at the moment it starts
- [ ] Verify the disclosure is visible on the first screen, not in a linked policy
- [ ] Confirm no covered system escapes because it is "just a rules-based assistant"

**If you are a health care provider:**
- [ ] Map every AI use that touches services or treatment
- [ ] Attach the disclosure to the intake workflow so it fires on the first date of service
- [ ] Write the emergency path — the disclosure still has to happen, just later
- [ ] Train staff on who delivers the disclosure and how it is documented

**If you are a private company:**
- [ ] Stop writing a TRAIGA disclosure duty into your compliance plan — the duty is not there
- [ ] Audit for the prohibitions instead, starting with intent evidence: what did your design documents and marketing materials say the system was for?
- [ ] Check whether you are an exempt insurer or federally insured financial institution, and document the basis
- [ ] Prepare for a 60-day cure demand, since that is how enforcement will start

---

## Frequently asked questions

**Does TRAIGA require private companies to disclose AI use?**
No. The disclosure duty applies to government entities interacting with consumers and to health care providers. Private companies are subject to the prohibitions, not to a disclosure mandate.

**When did TRAIGA take effect?**
January 1, 2026. It was signed June 22, 2025.

**Is disparate impact enough to violate TRAIGA?**
No. The act expressly states that disparate impact alone is not sufficient to show intent to discriminate. Intent must be shown.

**What is the maximum penalty?**
$200,000 per uncurable violation, with continuing violations at $2,000 to $40,000 per day.

**Can consumers sue under TRAIGA?**
No. Enforcement is exclusively the Attorney General's, with a 60-day cure period.

**Does TRAIGA override city AI ordinances?**
Yes. Texas preempts local government AI regulation, so TRAIGA is the statewide baseline.

---

**Related:** [Colorado SB 26-189: the disclosure law that does reach private companies](/colorado/sb-26-189/) · [Colorado vs Texas compared](/compare/colorado-vs-texas/) · [Which state laws are in effect now](/in-effect/)

*Last verified November 8, 2026. General information, not legal advice. Confirm against the enrolled bill text and Texas AG guidance.*


<!-- https://aidisclosurelaw.com/utah/ -->
# Utah's AI Disclosure Law Now Lives in Code Chapter 77

> **Short answer.** Utah's generative AI disclosure duty is in **Utah Code Title 13, Chapter 77**, in force since **May 7, 2025**. The original 2024 home for it — **§13-2-12** — was repealed by SB 226 and no longer exists. Chapter 77 sets two triggers: a **reactive** duty to disclose when a consumer in a consumer transaction clearly and unambiguously asks whether they are talking to AI, and a **proactive** duty for people in **licensed occupations** using generative AI in a **high-risk interaction** — verbal at the start of a verbal interaction, written before a written one. Violations are deceptive acts enforced by the Division of Consumer Protection: up to **$2,500** per violation administratively, up to **$5,000** per violation of an order.

---

## Why so many articles cite a dead section

SB 149 (2024) put the disclosure duty in **§13-2-12**. In 2025, SB 226 repealed that section and re-enacted a revised, narrower duty as its own chapter, **Title 13, Chapter 77**, "Generative Artificial Intelligence — Consumer Disclosures and Enforcement", effective **May 7, 2025**.

Two things went stale at once, and both are common online:

1. **The citation.** §13-2-12 is repealed. Compliance records, vendor questionnaires, and internal policies that cite it are pointing at nothing.
2. **The obligation.** The original law expected broad proactive disclosure of AI use. SB 226 narrowed the general-consumer duty to **disclosure on request only**, and confined proactive disclosure to licensed occupations in high-risk interactions.

Chapter 72 still exists — it holds the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy and the AI Learning Laboratory — and it is scheduled to sunset on **July 1, 2027**. That sunset does not, on its face, repeal the Chapter 77 disclosure duties. Do not let a vendor tell you Utah's rule disappears in 2027; that is the policy office, not the disclosure statute.

---

## Two triggers, two very different duties

| | General consumer | Licensed occupation |
|---|---|---|
| **Provision** | §13-77-103(1) | §13-77-103(2)–(3) |
| **Who** | Any "supplier" using generative AI to interact with an individual in connection with a consumer transaction | An individual providing services in a **regulated occupation** — one requiring a licence or state certification from the Department of Commerce |
| **Trigger** | The individual **clearly and unambiguously asks** whether they are interacting with AI rather than a human | The interaction is a **high-risk AI interaction** — no request needed |
| **Timing** | When asked | **Verbally at the start** of a verbal interaction; **in writing before** a written interaction |
| **Standard** | Truthful answer; never state that AI is a human | Prominent disclosure, up front |

### What makes an interaction "high risk"

Two elements, both required:

- Generative AI interactions involving **sensitive personal information** — health, financial, or biometric data
- **Personalised recommendations, advice, or information** that a person could reasonably rely on for a significant personal decision, including financial, legal, medical, or mental-health advice

That definition is narrower than it looks. Most retail chatbots, support bots, and marketing assistants never reach it. A licensed financial adviser's AI assistant discussing a client's retirement accounts does.

### What counts as generative AI

Chapter 77 covers AI trained on data, designed to simulate human conversation through text, audio, or visual communication, and generating **non-scripted, human-like output** with limited or no human oversight. A purely scripted or menu-driven bot sits outside the definition — which is why the definition of what you are running is the first question to answer, not the last.

---

## The safe harbour worth designing around

§13-77-104 gives you something unusual for an AI statute: a **practical way to stop worrying about the trigger**.

A person is not subject to enforcement for a §13-77-103 violation if the generative AI **clearly and conspicuously discloses at the outset, and throughout the interaction**, that it is generative AI, that it is not human, or that it is an AI assistant.

Note the "and throughout". A banner at the top of the chat that disappears after the first message is not this. Persistent identification — in the header, in each message block, in the voice preamble — is.

Practically: if you make the always-on disclosure, the reactive duty and the high-risk duty both stop mattering, because you have already disclosed. The reason to still separate them is the **non-disclosure case** — the vendor integration, the voice agent, the embedded assistant inside a partner's product.

---

## Penalties and enforcement

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Regulator | Division of Consumer Protection, Utah Department of Commerce |
| Theory | A deceptive act or practice under the Consumer Sales Practices Act |
| Administrative fine | Up to **$2,500** per violation |
| Civil penalty | Up to **$5,000** per violation of an administrative or court order |
| Other remedies | Injunctive relief, disgorgement of profits, the Division's fees and costs |
| Criminal exposure | None |
| "The model did it" | **Not a defence.** Chapter 77 states generative AI is not a defence where the AI made the statement, took the act, or was used in furtherance of the violation |

Per-violation structure means exposure scales with conversation volume, not with company size. A single deployment answering thousands of consumer chats weekly is a different risk profile from one human-supervised agent.

---

## The question nobody has answered: does this reach hiring?

Utah's chapter is a **consumer protection** statute, not an employment one, and it says nothing about job applicants.

The honest analysis:

- The proactive duty is limited to **regulated occupations**. Recruiting and HR are not licensed occupations in Utah, so §13-77-103(2) is very unlikely to reach an ordinary hiring process on its own terms.
- The reactive duty turns on whether a job application is a **consumer transaction**. Chapter 77 borrows that definition from the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act (§13-11-3), which describes a sale, lease, or transfer of goods or services to a person for personal, family, or household purposes. An application is not obviously a purchase by the applicant.
- No Division of Consumer Protection guidance applies the chapter to hiring.

If you want the risk gone rather than analysed, the safe harbour solves it: disclose that the interviewer or screener is AI, persistently. A hiring chatbot that says what it is has no disclosure question left to argue about.

---

## Mental-health chatbots are a separate, heavier track

If the product is a mental-health chatbot offered to Utah users, Chapter 77 is not your main obligation. **Title 13, Chapter 72a** (from HB 452, 2025) requires disclosure that the chatbot is artificial intelligence and not human:

- **Before** features are accessed
- At the beginning of an interaction **after a seven-day gap**
- Whenever a Utah user asks or prompts about whether AI is being used

It also restricts selling or sharing a user's chatbot input and individually identifiable health information. Different chapter, different regulator posture, and a disclosure schedule that no generic chatbot banner satisfies.

---

## Implementation checklist

- [ ] Replace every citation of §13-2-12 with Title 13, Chapter 77
- [ ] Classify each conversational system: scripted (outside), generative (inside)
- [ ] For each generative system, decide which tier it is in — general consumer, regulated occupation high-risk, or mental-health chatbot
- [ ] Test whether the bot answers "am I talking to a human" truthfully in its own words, and how it handles indirect phrasings
- [ ] Either build the always-on safe-harbour disclosure, or build the per-tier trigger logic — not neither
- [ ] Make the disclosure persistent, not a first-message banner
- [ ] If you serve licensed professionals, put the disclosure in writing *before* the written interaction begins, and script it into the verbal opening
- [ ] Re-check the text each general session; chapter 77 has already been amended once and chapter 72 sunsets July 1, 2027

---

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Utah Code §13-2-12 still law?**
No. SB 226 (2025) repealed it and re-enacted the disclosure duty as Title 13, Chapter 77, effective May 7, 2025. Anything citing §13-2-12 for a current obligation is out of date.

**Does Utah require AI disclosure even if the customer does not ask?**
Only for individuals in a licensed occupation making a high-risk AI interaction, and for mental-health chatbots under chapter 72a. For ordinary consumer interactions the duty is reactive: you disclose when the person clearly and unambiguously asks.

**What is a high-risk AI interaction?**
Generative AI that involves sensitive personal information — health, financial, or biometric — and produces personalised recommendations or advice a person could reasonably rely on for a significant decision, including financial, legal, medical, or mental-health matters.

**Is there a safe harbour?**
Yes. Persistent, conspicuous disclosure at the outset and throughout that the system is generative AI and not human removes the enforcement exposure under §13-77-104.

**Does the July 2027 sunset kill the disclosure duty?**
No. The sunset applies to chapter 72, which houses the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy and the learning laboratory. Chapter 77 is separate and is not repealed by that date.

**Does this apply to a hiring chatbot?**
Unresolved. The proactive duty is limited to licensed occupations, and whether a job application is a "consumer transaction" has not been decided. Disclose persistently and the question stops mattering.
